title: What Makes Something a 'Task'? Defining the Core Concept
brief: Define a TBLT 'task' by contrasting it with a conventional grammar exercise: a task requires learners to use language to achieve a real, communicable outcome rather than to display a linguistic form. Draw on the source's description of student-centered learning—where 'students then work together to practice, using the language for real communicative purposes'—and its definition of rationale, explaining that tasks carry a built-in need to know. Use the source's discussion of driving questions and the idea that students 'see the need to gain knowledge, understand concepts, and apply skills' to illustrate what 'real outcome' means in practice. Do NOT discuss lesson staging or research evidence here; those are covered in later sections.

title: How a TBLT Lesson Is Structured: Pre-Task, Task Cycle, and Post-Task
brief: Walk through the three-phase architecture of a TBLT lesson. For the pre-task phase, draw on the source's concept of an 'Entry Event that generates interest and curiosity' and the idea of establishing a need to know. For the task cycle, use the source's descriptions of group work, student voice and choice, and in-depth inquiry ('a rigorous, extended process of asking questions, using resources, and developing answers'). For the post-task or report phase, draw on the source's emphasis on debriefing—'brings closure to the activity; it helps the teacher check for student comprehension'—and on public audience ('students present their work to other people, beyond their classmates and teacher'). Keep the focus on lesson flow; save assessment tools for the next section.

title: Scaffolding and Assessment Inside a TBLT Classroom
brief: Explain how teachers support learners during tasks without taking over the communicative work. Use the source's definition of scaffolding—'teachers prepare, present, and/or guide students through a series of progressively more complex steps'—and its description of the teacher as 'guide on the side' rather than 'sage on the stage.' Then cover how task performance is assessed: draw on the source's treatment of rubrics ('scoring guide or template for assessing/providing feedback on student work and performance that is clearly linked to learning objectives'), checklists, and peer assessment. Use the sample project rubric criteria from the source (participation, vocabulary use, pronunciation, audience questions) as a concrete illustration of what TBLT assessment looks like in practice.

title: The Research Base: What Meta-Analyses Tell Us
brief: Present the quantitative evidence for TBLT honestly and in full. Introduce Bryfonski & McKay (2019) as the field's landmark meta-analysis of 52 studies, reporting a positive effect of d = 0.93 (Bryfonski & McKay, 2019). Then immediately present Xuan, Cheung & Liu (2025) as a re-analysis of the same body of evidence: correcting for loose inclusion criteria, they report a more modest g = 0.61, which is the figure learners should treat as the current best estimate (Xuan, Cheung & Liu, 2025). Explain what 'effect size' means in plain language so non-specialist readers can interpret both numbers. Make clear that the direction of the effect—TBLT outperforms comparison conditions—is not in dispute; only the magnitude is contested. Do not invent any additional statistics or claims beyond these two verified citations.

title: Why the Numbers Differ: Inclusion Criteria and What They Mean for Teachers
brief: Unpack the methodological reason the two meta-analyses reach different conclusions: Xuan et al. (2025) argue that Bryfonski & McKay (2019) applied loose inclusion criteria, pulling in studies that may not represent pure TBLT, which inflated the original d = 0.93. Use this contrast to teach a transferable research-literacy lesson—that effect sizes are only as trustworthy as the studies feeding them. Connect back to the source's emphasis on rationale: teachers who understand why a method works (or how confidently we know it works) are better placed to explain their choices to students and adapt intelligently. Remind readers that g = 0.61 still represents a meaningful, positive effect and that the honest position is: direction settled, magnitude contested (Xuan, Cheung & Liu, 2025; Bryfonski & McKay, 2019).

title: Putting It Together: Applying TBLT Principles in Your Classroom
brief: Synthesise the unit by guiding readers through the practical steps of designing a TBLT lesson for their own context. Draw on the source's action-plan framework: choosing materials that connect to student interests, designing activities around integrated language skills, incorporating pair and group work, and producing 'a defined end product or performance outcome.' Use the source's Project-based Learning Essential Elements Checklist criteria—significant content, 21st-century skills, revision and reflection, public audience—as a planning checklist that operationalises TBLT principles. Close by acknowledging the honest evidence position established in the previous two sections: teachers can adopt TBLT with reasonable confidence in a positive effect while remaining alert to context factors the meta-analyses cannot capture.
